newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Namibia suspends plans to tap Okavango.
newsitem.headline: Namibia suspends plans to tap Okavango.

text.p: Following good rains Namibia's cabinet has suspended controversial plans to tap the Okavango River, but said a pipeline was still needed in the long term, Information Minister Ben Amathila said.

"Cabinet considered the findings of the feasibility study into the emergency link from the Okavango River to Grootfontein and resolved that due to the good inflows to the dams, the pipeline construction project no longer needs to be considered as a humaniarian crisis", Amathila told reporters on Wednesday.

But he said the need for the 250 km (155 mile) pipeline from Rundu on the Okavango to Grootfontein, where it will link up with the existing pipeline network supplying the capital Windhoek, still remained.
Conservationists have blasted Namibia's plans to drain the waters of the Okavango River saying it will disrupt the delicate ecosystem of the Okavango Delta in neighbouring Botswana.
The delta, the world's largest, is Botswana's main tourist destination.

"The Okavango River-Grootfontein pipeline link requires to be further investigated immediately in terms of a detailed design ... for possible implementation within the next four-and-a-half years," Amathila said.
He said the Namibian government would continue consultations with its neighbours, Angola and Botswana, on the issue.
Botswana's permanent secretary for the Ministry of Mineral Resources and Water Affairs, Blackie Marole, welcomed Namibia's decision.
"We have always agreed that if Namibia decided to follow the option of extracting water from the Okavango it must first make sure there was a thorough environmental study," he told Reuters.
"With the recent rains in Namibia, they now have time to wait for the OKACOM (Okavango Basin Commission) survey to be completed," he added.

OKACOM is an association of Angola, Namibia and Botswana, the basin states of the river, set up in 1995. It commissioned a detailed environmental and technical survey on the use of water from the river.

Meanwhile, Namibia's Agriculture, Water and Rural Development Minister Helmuth Angula has tabled a motion in parliament to emphasise the importance of agreements on shared water sources to help develop Namibia's economy.
